extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style guide listing preferred terms, discouraged usages, and reporting guidance for describing identities, cultures, disabilities, religions, and other sensitive topics in news copy. It instructs reporters when to use labels, which words to avoid, and offers context and definitions to ensure accurate, respectful coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: bipolar disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Formerly known as manic depression, this mental illness is believed to be caused by a combination of genetic factors and neurological functioning... It is characterized by unusually intense shifts in emotion, energy, behavior and activity levels in what are called 'mood episodes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having bipolar disorder only if the information is central to the story and a licensed medical professional has formally diagnosed the person. Do not use bipolar as an adjective for something that rapidly or drastically changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: biracial, multiracial, mixed-race, two or more races
rubrics_metrics.description: Biracial refers to people of two races; multiracial refers to people of two or more racial backgrounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred terms include multiracial, biracial, multiethnic, polyethnic. Use mixed and mixed-race with caution as some people find these terms offensive; however, others embrace them.

rubrics_metrics.name: birth defect
rubrics_metrics.description: See defect/birth defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: bisexual, bi
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who has the capacity to form enduring physical, romantic and/or emotional attractions to those of the same gender or to those of another gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People may experience this attraction in differing ways and degrees over their lifetime. Bisexual people need not have had specific sexual experiences to be bisexual; in fact, they need not have had any sexual experience at all to identify as bisexual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Africa
rubrics_metrics.description: See Africa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black church
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective noun that refers to the more than 65,000 Christian churches that have a predominance of Black members and clerical leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Black Church has served as a major institutional foundation in the Black community. It generally refers to Protestants and does not generally encompass Catholics, Muslims or others. In some cases 'Black churches' may be more accurate; be mindful many Black people worldwide belong to churches and denominations that are not predominantly Black.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes curtailing the rights of African Americans during the early years of Reconstruction and instituted by Southern legislative bodies in 1865 and 1866.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also known as Negro Codes; statutes aimed to restore political powers and economic structure of slavery, for example by forbidding Black people from owning or renting farmland.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black diaspora
rubrics_metrics.description: See African diaspora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black English, African American English
rubrics_metrics.description: See Ebonics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black leader
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It implies that one person is the spokesperson for all Black people. When referring to a local Black person in a leadership position, state the organization that he or she belongs to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Lives Matter, #BlackLivesMatter
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil rights movement that started after the July 2013 acquittal of George Zimmerman... started as a Twitter hashtag by Alicia Garza, Patrisse Cullors and Opal Tometi as 'a call to action and a response to the virulent anti-Black racism that permeates our society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: According to its website, #BlackLivesMatter does not believe Black lives are more important than other lives and stands with other oppressed peoples. The campaign opposes police violence against Black people and views unequal threats faced by Black people as a reason for the movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Muslim
rubrics_metrics.description: Black Muslim is a term that became associated with the Nation of Islam but is now considered derogatory and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred term is simply 'member of the Nation of Islam.' Do not use 'Black Muslim' to describe African-Americans who practice traditional Islam; instead say African-American Muslims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black or African American, U.S. Census definition of
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Census Bureau defines Black or African American as 'a person having origins in any of the Black racial groups of Africa.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The racial categories reflect a social definition of race recognized in this country and are not an attempt to define race biologically, anthropologically, or genetically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Twitter
rubrics_metrics.description: A virtual community on the Twitter social network that focuses on issues of interest to the Black community, particularly in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Black Twitter has been used as a tool for social activism, such as organizing protest rallies and boycotts.

rubrics_metrics.name: black, Black
rubrics_metrics.description: See African American, African-American, black, Black.

rubrics_metrics.name: blind/limited vision/low vision/partially sighted/visually impaired
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the American Foundation for the Blind, 'legally blind' denotes a person with 20/200 visual acuity or less. Many people with vision loss are not considered blind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'blind' only when the person has complete loss of sight and 'legally blind' when the person has almost complete loss of sight. Otherwise use limited vision, low vision, partially sighted, or visually impaired as appropriate. Ask the person which term they prefer. Note regional differences (e.g., 'partially sighted' in British usage) and that some may object to 'visually impaired' because it describes condition in terms of a deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bollywood
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indian movie industry’s equivalent of Hollywood; a popular term for Hindi cinema and a vast pop culture industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bollywood is not the only source of Indian cinema; movies are made in other languages. Bollywood movies often are musicals with singing and dancing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bombay
rubrics_metrics.description: See Mumbai.

rubrics_metrics.name: boomer
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes a person who was born during the post-World War II baby boom between 1946 and 1964.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Boomers' and 'boomer generation' preferred over 'baby boomers,' which is perceived as condescending. Do not lump the entire generation together unless appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boricua
rubrics_metrics.description: Puerto Rico was formerly known as Borikén; the term Boricua is a derivative and connotes pride in Puerto Rican origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: born-again
rubrics_metrics.description: Theologically, all Christians claim to be born-again through the saving work of Jesus Christ; different traditions disagree over how it occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the term tends to associate someone with a particular religious tradition, do not label someone a 'born-again Christian.' Let the person label themselves, e.g., 'who calls herself a born-again Christian.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Borscht Belt
rubrics_metrics.description: Informal term for the summer resorts of the Catskill Mountains that primarily catered to Ashkenazic Jewish families in the mid-20th century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides historical and cultural context; networks of bungalow colonies and hotels supported Black entertainers and Jewish performers; reference to cultural artifacts like 'Dirty Dancing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Buddha
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'BUD-dah'... The Buddha, meaning 'the awakened one,' refers to Siddhartha Gautama, the founder of Buddhism. A Buddha is anyone who has attained enlightenment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are human Buddhas of the past, present and future as well as celestial Buddhas venerated in some schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buddhism
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth-largest organized religion in the world founded in India between the sixth and fifth centuries B.C., based on the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes core beliefs (meditation, moral behavior, rebirth, nirvana) and major forms: Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana, with brief descriptions of each and their geographic associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: burkini
rubrics_metrics.description: A type of swimming suit that covers the arms, legs and hair and is worn by some Muslim women; a mix of the words burqa and bikini.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some Muslim women choose it to demonstrate modesty and faith. Note that in 2016 some towns in France banned women from wearing a burkini on public beaches after terrorist attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burmese names
rubrics_metrics.description: Naming rules are complex; names typically consist of two one-syllable names, often with an honorific (Daw, Maa, Naw, Saw, Maung, U).

rubrics_metrics.name: burqa
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of covering for women who are Muslims, most frequently found in Afghanistan and Pakistan; an all-enveloping outer garment with a net-covered opening for the eyes or face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See abaya, hijab and niqab for related terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: C.E.
rubrics_metrics.description: See A.D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cajun, Creole
rubrics_metrics.description: Cajun is a native of Louisiana descended from Acadian French immigrants. Creole is a person of European parentage born in the West Indies, Central America, tropical South America or the Gulf States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cambodian names
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically family name first, personal name second. Middle names are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantonese
rubrics_metrics.description: A dialect mainly spoken in the environs of Canton (Guangzhou), principal dialect of Hong Kong; not spoken by all Chinese.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Mandarin.

rubrics_metrics.name: caste
rubrics_metrics.description: For hundreds of years India had a caste system of social hierarchy with roots in Hindu scriptures; it evolved into a hereditary and hierarchical structure limiting social mobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in law since independence removed many vestiges, but caste persists and forms the basis for quotas and affirmative-action policies. Note that Indians in the United States do not use a caste system.

rubrics_metrics.name: caste system
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional social, economic and religious structure of Indian society dividing people into varna and jati, which became a rigid hereditary hierarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although caste discrimination is illegal and many leaders say it's not sanctioned by Hinduism, it persists and created categories like 'untouchables' (Scheduled Castes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Catholic, catholic
rubrics_metrics.description: When capitalized, refers specifically to the Roman Catholic Church. Lowercase 'catholic' means universal or worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most Roman Catholics are Western/Latin Catholics, but the Roman Catholic Church includes 22 Eastern Catholic churches. Never refer to Eastern Catholics as Orthodox or vice versa; use 'Roman Catholic' if a distinction is being made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caucasian
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid as a synonym for White, unless used in demographic data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Updated guidance (Feb 2021) — prefer more precise terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central America
rubrics_metrics.description: A tropical isthmus connecting North and South America, bordered by Mexico, Colombia, the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean; consists of seven countries: Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Panama.

rubrics_metrics.name: cerebral palsy
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of neurological disorders that appear in infancy or early childhood and permanently affect body movement and muscle coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to describe a person as 'someone with cerebral palsy,' followed by a short explanation. When describing specific symptoms, ask the person what terms they prefer. It's acceptable to refer to 'spastic cerebral palsy' but derogatory to call someone 'spastic' or 'a spaz.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Chabad
rubrics_metrics.description: The official organization of the Chabad-Lubavitch movement of Judaism, based in Crown Heights, N.Y.; a branch of Hasidism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chabad emphasizes outreach to nonpracticing Jews; the term comes from a Hebrew acronym for wisdom, understanding and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chaldeans
rubrics_metrics.description: Catholics from Iraq; a religious and ethnic minority with large U.S. communities in Detroit and San Diego.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chaldean Catholic Church has had connections with the Roman Catholic Church since 1551 and been affiliated since 1830. Chaldeans and Assyrians, along with Arabs, are Semite people; cultural foundation is similar but religious affiliation differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charlie Chan
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution. Stereotype. Created in 1925; became the protagonist in many Hollywood films and was played by white actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chan spoke 'inscrutable' dialogue and perpetuated stereotypes. Use caution when referencing such characters and their problematic history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chican@
rubrics_metrics.description: A post-internet construction simplifying 'Chicano/Chicana' used in some academic department names; uses '@' ending to present both feminine and masculine endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Latin@.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chicana, Chicano
rubrics_metrics.description: People of Mexican descent; Chicano refers to men and Chicana to women. Originally derogatory, later adopted by the Chicano movement as a term of pride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Latina, Latino.

rubrics_metrics.name: chief
rubrics_metrics.description: Has multiple meanings; when used to refer to a leader or ruler of a people or clan, make sure the word is appropriate and actually used by that group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never use as a nickname for a Native man; 'chief' as a nickname can be insulting. Also recognize other meanings (chief engineer, CEO) and slang usages; avoid slang that perpetuates stereotypes unless part of a quote.

rubrics_metrics.name: china doll
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution. A figurine, usually porcelain; when used metaphorically it demeans women of Chinese or Asian heritage by implying submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See reverse image of sexual dominance in Dragon Lady; avoid pejorative metaphorical usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinaman
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid. A slur, often applied to anyone of Asian heritage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term dates to 19th-century America; avoid usage and related phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese laundries
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution. Can be racially charged; historical context of Chinese laundries opening in 1851 and their economic role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of racial connotations and historical discrimination (e.g., Chinese once permitted to own only restaurants and laundries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese names
rubrics_metrics.description: Typically family name first, personal name second. Many Chinese Americans change word order to conform to Western practice and may adopt Western names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal names sometimes hyphenated; check if the interview subject prefers a hyphen. See South Asian names for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: ching-chong
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid. A slur. Similar to chink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See chink; do not use.

rubrics_metrics.name: chink
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid. A slur. Similar to Chinaman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid phrases such as 'chink in the armor' that call to mind the slur. See Chinaman, ching-chong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chitlin' Circuit
rubrics_metrics.description: A touring route Black entertainers used in the early 20th century providing safe venues and lodging during Jim Crow discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Played a role in development of music genres like the blues and rock ’n’ roll and supported Black businesses; historical examples and notable performers listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: chopsticks
rubrics_metrics.description: Originated in China around 1200 B.C.; moved from stove to table and became popular in China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People in Indonesia, Thailand and India don’t traditionally use chopsticks. Some Southeast Asian restaurants offer them despite not being traditional in those cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christianity
rubrics_metrics.description: The world’s largest religion based on the life and teachings of Jesus as described in the New Testament; Christians consider Jesus the Son of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes historical separation from Judaism and the spread of Christianity via Apostle Paul; contextual guidance when reporting on faith traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
rubrics_metrics.description: The church asks journalists to use the proper name and discourages 'Mormon Church' or calling adherents 'Mormons.' The official name is The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First reference: full name preferred; shortened references 'the Church' or 'the Church of Jesus Christ' encouraged. Avoid 'LDS' or 'Mormon' as substitutes. When referring to members, use 'members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' or 'Latter-day Saints.' 'Mormon' is acceptable in proper names (Book of Mormon) and some historical expressions. Note that the church is not affiliated with polygamous groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cinco de Mayo
rubrics_metrics.description: A Mexican holiday recalling victory over France in the 1862 Battle of Puebla.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Festivities include parades, mariachi music, and special foods. In the U.S., it's considered a celebration of Mexican culture; it is not equivalent to the Fourth of July. Mexico's Independence Day is Sept. 16.

rubrics_metrics.name: cisgender, cis
rubrics_metrics.description: A term used by some to describe people who are not transgender; 'cis-' is a Latin prefix meaning 'on the same side as.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A more widely understood way to describe people who are not transgender is simply 'non-transgender people.' Note NLGJA guidance that 'cisgender' may be shortened to 'cis' and combined as ciswoman or cisman, and that the word distinguishes without assuming cisgender is the neutral or normal state.

rubrics_metrics.name: civil rights movement, Civil Rights Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Often used to describe struggles of Black Americans between 1945 and 1970 to end discrimination and segregation; Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize with events like Montgomery bus boycott, sit-ins, and the March on Washington in 1963.

rubrics_metrics.name: civil union
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal status providing same-sex couples some rights available to married couples in areas such as state taxes, medical decisions and estate planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil unions have been recognized by some states but not the U.S. government. See commitment ceremony and domestic partner. Note: on June 26, 2015 the Supreme Court ruled Constitution guarantees the right to marry; marriage equality is the law of the land.

rubrics_metrics.name: classism
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudiced thoughts and discriminatory actions based on socioeconomic status, income or class, usually by upper classes against people of lower socioeconomic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: closed captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed captions are captions on a video intended for audience members who are Deaf or have hearing loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They provide text of all audible information, including spoken words and captions describing loud noises, sound effects and music.

rubrics_metrics.name: closeted, in the closet
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes a person who is not open about his or her sexual orientation or gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better to simply refer to someone as not out about being lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender. Some individuals may be out to some people but not others due to fear of rejection, harassment, violence, or job loss. See coming out, outing.

rubrics_metrics.name: cochlear implant
rubrics_metrics.description: An electronic device that can help a person who is deaf or hard of hearing; does not fully restore hearing but gives a representation of sounds to help a person understand speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid describing it as a corrective device or one that would restore a deaf person to mainstream society. Define it as an electronic device that can assist a person who is deaf or hard of hearing in understanding speech. See Deaf/deaf and note community perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: code switching
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing the way one speaks depending on the situation at hand; within the Black community, some people speak differently with friends than with family or at work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code switching is a learned skill and requires dedicated, well-trained teachers and long-term experience to master. Describe context: youth from families where African American Language is dominant will enter school speaking AAL, and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: coded language
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting terms related to race or racial identity with seemingly race-neutral terms that disguise explicit and/or implicit bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'inner-city' and 'urban' as code for Black people, people of color or low-income people.

rubrics_metrics.name: codeswitching
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting between two or more different languages, dialects, accents or modes of speaking or modifying one’s behavior or appearance to adapt to different situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: codger
rubrics_metrics.description: Ageist terminology. Avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: colonialism
rubrics_metrics.description: European Age of Exploration led to subjugation of less technologically advanced peoples as European colonies; many countries of Asia, Africa, Americas were colonized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Imperialism, Third World; note consequences like shedding of empire after WWII and the persistence of colonial legacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: colored
rubrics_metrics.description: An archaic term for Black; in some African countries 'colored' denotes those of mixed racial ancestry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use unless referring to official names, historical events or in quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: colorism
rubrics_metrics.description: Occurs when someone with lighter skin is favored over someone with darker skin; exists within all races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: the 'brown paper bag test' among African Americans. Be aware of internal community dynamics and discrimination based on skin tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: coming out
rubrics_metrics.description: Short for 'coming out of the closet.' Accepting and letting others know of one’s previously hidden sexual orientation or gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See closeted/in the closet, outing.

rubrics_metrics.name: commitment ceremony
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal, marriage-like ceremony in which two people declare their commitment to each other; individuals can be of the same or different sexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceremonies may be religiously recognized but are not legally binding. See civil union, domestic partner.

rubrics_metrics.name: community
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution. A synonym for a neighborhood or town, but a cliché; implies a shared like-mindedness that no reporter can possibly confirm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid broad phrases like 'the Korean community' or 'white community leaders.' Better to identify leaders and ethnically based groups by name and reference size of membership when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confucianism
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosophy developed by Confucius emphasizing social harmony and moral obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify as a philosophy, not a religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: congenital disability
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who has a congenital disability has had a disability since birth; examples include Down syndrome and heart-related conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'a person with a congenital disability,' 'has had a disability since birth,' or 'was born with a disability.' Name specific disability only when pertinent. Avoid terms like 'defect' or 'birth' that imply the person is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: continuing care retirement community
rubrics_metrics.description: A community that offers several levels of assistance including independent living, assisted living and skilled nursing care, usually on one campus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These communities usually offer long-term contracts or written agreements between resident and community.

rubrics_metrics.name: convict
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid this term when referring to a person who is incarcerated or has been convicted of a crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, use people-first language. (Text cuts off with reference to The Marshall Project.)
